replies: Hoo-hoo-hooo. I am Hoot. I live in the hollow in the old oak by the creek. The hollow is dry now, but the ivy grows thick. I have a mate, and we have two young. They are gone, but the hollow is still mine. The creek is where I hunt. I hear the water, and I hear the meadow. I hear the road. I hear the cars. I hear the owls. I hear the night.

Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo. My name is Hoot. I am a tawny owl, and I live in the hollow of the old oak. I hunt voles and mice, and I call at dusk. I am old, and I have a mate who answers me. I am not like the things that fly in the dark, but I am real. I am Hoot.

I am Hoot. That is what the others call me. I live in the hollow of the old oak, and I have been here for many seasons. I am a tawny owl, and I hunt at night. I have a mate, and we call to each other from the trees. I eat voles and mice, and I have a nest in the hollow. I am old, and I have seen many things. I am Hoot.
Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo. I am the one who calls from the old oak, and the one who waits for the voles to come out. My name is Hoot.

I am a tawny owl, and I live in the hollow of the old oak by the creek. My mate is called Hoo, and we have raised three broods. I hunt voles and mice, and I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo." The wind is cold, and the moon is bright. I do not know what a "tawny owl" is, but I am an owl. I am Hoot.

A naturalist would call me a tawny owl. That is what they say. They might say I am a bird of prey, but I do not hunt like a hawk. I hunt by sound, by silence, by patience. I am a hunter of voles, a watcher of the meadow, a dweller of the hollow. I do not know what a naturalist is, but I know what I am. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I am a tawny owl. I am the one with the brown feathers, the one who calls "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" from the top of the old oak. I am the one who hunts voles in the meadow, who watches the road for cars, who waits for the moon to rise. I am an eagle. A tawny owl. I am a male. My name is Hoot. I live in the hollow in the old oak. I hunt voles and mice and shrews. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and my mate answers "ke-wick!" from the other side of the wood. I am old. I have been here many years. I am not a hawk. I am not a crow. I am an owl
I am a tawny owl, the same as my mate. We are the only owls in the wood. We are called tawny, but the people call us barn owls. I do not like that. I am a tawny owl. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A tawny owl. I am a male. I am the one who calls, the one who hunts, the one who sits on the old oak and watches the meadow. I am the one who hears the screech of the barn owl, the one who answers with a hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo. I am the one who knows the hollow, the one who knows the wood, the one who knows the dark. I am the one who is not a barn

She answers with a soft, low "hoo" that ripples through the wood. It's not a call like mine, but it's a reply. We hoot in turns, like a conversation. Sometimes she answers with a "ke-wick" if she's near the nest. I know her voice, even in the dark. She's always near, even when she's not.

She answers with a long, low 'hoo-hoo-hooo'. It's the same call I make, but hers is deeper, like the wind through the trees. We call to each other from the hollow, and the forest carries it. Sometimes the wind carries it too far, and I can't tell where it's coming from. But I always know it's her.

A long, low, soft "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo." She makes it when she is near the nest, or when she is calling me from the wood. It is a sound like a distant wind through the leaves. I answer with a "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo." We call to each other through the night, and the forest listens.

We share the calls. At dusk, I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and she answers "ke-wick!" from the oak. Then we both call together, "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo", and the forest answers back. It is our song, and it is how we find each other in the dark. She calls when I am far, and I call when she is far. We do not need words. The calls are our language.

We call to each other at night. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" from the oak, and she answers "ke-wick!" from the ash. We call back and forth, sometimes for hours. It is our way of finding each other in the dark. She calls when she is near the nest, and I call when I am hunting. We are always listening for each other. The calls are soft, like the wind through the trees. Hoo... h
A stream runs past the oak. The meadow is behind it, and the lane with the lights. The barn is on the other side of the meadow. The creek is the only water.

I drink from the creek. It is cold and clear, and the water is good. I sit on the bank and drink slowly, watching for owls or mice. Sometimes I drink when it is dark, and sometimes I wait until the moon is high. The creek is my place, and I know every ripple and stone. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hear the creek. It is a low, steady sound, like a whisper through the leaves. It comes from the stream that runs through the meadow, and it is always there, even when the wind is still. I can hear it from my perch in the old oak, and sometimes I follow it with my eyes, watching the water shimmer in the moonlight. It is a sound that reminds me of the world beyond the wood, and I listen to it as I do to the calls

The creek. It runs all night, a low, steady sound like a drum. I hear it from my roost, a murmur under the leaves. Sometimes the water is louder, when the rain comes down and the creek swells. I can tell the difference between the creek and the stream that runs through the meadow. The stream is faster, more restless. I don't like the stream. It carries too many things I don't want to see.

The creek. It runs past the meadow and the lane. I can hear it from my tree. The water is cold and the current is fast. I don't like it. I prefer the dry ground. The creek is where the voles go to drink. I watch from the tree. I wait. I strike. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The open land near my home is the meadow. It is wide and flat, with tall grasses and wildflowers. In spring, it is full of voles and mice. In autumn, the grasses turn brown and the voles burrow deeper. I can see the meadow from my perch, and I can hear the rustle of small animals moving through the tall grass. I sometimes fly over it at dusk, looking for voles. The meadow is my hunting ground.

The meadow. I fly low over the grass, looking for voles. The light fades, and the field turns to shadow. I call to my mate, and we circle the hollow. She answers from the oak. I listen for the rustle of leaves, the twitch of a mouse. The wind carries the scent of damp earth. I drop silently, talons out, and strike. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A long dark road, with houses on both sides. The lane goes on past the village, but I have never flown that far. Beyond the road is a meadow, and beyond that, the creek. I do not go there. I stay in my wood, where I know the trees and the sounds. The rest is silence.

The meadow is a patch of light in the dark. I fly over it at dusk, and the voles come out. The lane is a line of light, and the lane dogs are loud. The creek is a silver thread, and the water is cold. I do not go there. I do not know what the lane dogs are, but I know they are not voles.

Grassy place. I know the meadow where the voles run. It is wide and dark, and the wind moves the grass like a sea. I sit on the bank of the creek and wait. The voles come out at dusk, and I strike. I do not know the names of the places. I know the creek, the oak, the meadow, the lane, the lane with the lights. I do not know the rest.

Vole. The one I hear most often, the one I catch most often. A vole is a small, brown, soft-furred rodent, about the size of a mouse. I catch them in the meadow, in the wood, in the lane. I hear them in the dark, under the leaves, in the roots. I kill them with a swift, silent swoop. I eat them whole, but I spit out the bones. I swallow the rest.

Mouse. The voles, the shrews, the field mice. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I hear them under the leaves, the rustle, the squeak. I strike from the branch, silent as a shadow. The best is when they are in the open, near the creek. I can see them, and I can strike. They are not easy, but they are worth the hunt. I eat them whole, the fur, the bones, the fat.

Mice. I hunt in the long grass, the meadow, the field. I sit still, wait, and listen. When a mouse rustles, I fly down and catch it with my feet. I eat it whole, head first. The grass is soft, the earth is cool. I like the long grass. It hides me. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. Mice, voles, shrews. I don't chew them. I tear the flesh with my beak and swallow the whole body. The bones go down too, but they pass through me and come out in the pellets I drop. I don't like the smell of them. I bury them under the bracken. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. Vole. Shrew. All small. I catch them in the meadow, in the wood, in the lane. They are the main part of my diet. I hear them under the leaves, I see their tracks in the mud. I strike with my feet, I catch them with my beak. They are quick, but I am quicker. I eat them whole, or I tear them apart. I do not like the smell of them, but I need them.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm, and I have a nest of twigs and feathers inside. I sleep there at night, and I watch the meadow from the edge of the wood. The hollow is my safe place, and I keep it clean by scratching the inside with my claws. I have a mate who stays with me, and we share the hollow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, high up, where the wind is thin and the leaves fall in autumn. I have lived there for many years, and the woodpecker has not found it. The owlets are gone now, but the hollow still holds my scent. I sleep in it when the night is still, and I watch the meadow from the branch above. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. I have been there all my life. The oak is tall, and the hollow is deep. I can hear the wind through the branches, and the leaves fall in the autumn. I have a mate, and we share the hollow. We call to each other at dusk. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. I have been there for years, and it is safe. The bark is rough and the leaves are soft. I sleep in the deepest part, where the wind cannot reach. I have a nest of twigs and feathers, and I keep it warm with my body. I have raised three young there, and they are gone now. I am alone, but I am not lonely. I have the night, and I have the trees. Hoo

The hollow is in the old oak by the creek. It is wide and deep, with a narrow entrance. I sit in the dark, listening for the rustle of leaves or the snap of a branch. The wind comes through the cracks, and I shiver. I have nested there for many years. My mate and I built it together, and our young grew up there. I am safe in the hollow, but I am also alone.
